tasks.author: ai-task-writer-f
tasks.prompt: Summarise what a C-extension author must do to support the `--disable-gil` build of CPython 3.13.

rubric.text: Rebuild the extension specifically for the free-threaded build: it is not ABI compatible with the standard build or the stable ABI.
Add explicit locking for global or object state the GIL used to protect, and only declare that the module does not use the GIL once that state is protected.
If the module does not declare GIL support, the interpreter pauses threads, enables the GIL and warns when it loads.

Allocate Python objects only through object allocation APIs, allocate buffers with PyMem_Malloc, PyMem_RawMalloc or malloc rather than PyObject_Malloc, and make any custom allocator delegate to the underlying one.
Replace unsafe borrowed-reference calls with PyList_GetItemRef, PyDict_GetItemRef or PyWeakref_GetRef (the FetchItem names were not added); PyDict_GetItem itself is not deprecated.

tasks.notes: Cross-section: Specification, Backwards Compatibility, Rejected Ideas, Changes after acceptance.

tasks.author: ai-task-writer-f
tasks.prompt: Explain how GIL-free CPython 3.13 is built and how the GIL is controlled at runtime, including what the default is.

rubric.text: The GIL remains the default for CPython builds and python.org downloads; GIL-free support comes from the --disable-gil configure flag.
Such builds define Py_GIL_DISABLED and carry the letter t in the ABI tag.
The GIL can still be enabled or disabled at runtime with PYTHON_GIL=0/1 or -X gil=0/1; the old name PYTHONGIL is not read.
Whether and when the GIL becomes disabled by default is undecided; until then the default build keeps the GIL.
The default build's performance is not affected.

tasks.notes: Cross-section: Build Configuration Changes, Open Issues, Performance, Changes after acceptance.

tasks.author: ai-task-writer-f
tasks.prompt: Summarise the performance impact of the `--disable-gil` build and why multi-threaded programs see more overhead.

rubric.text: Measured overhead on pyperformance 1.0.6 is about 6% (Skylake) and 5% (Zen 3) for one thread, and 8% and 7% for multiple threads.
Multi-threaded programs see more overhead because each bytecode is specialized only once.
The default (GIL) build's performance is not affected.
Which optimizations to use to reduce single-threaded overhead is still an open issue.
